title: The Shattered Veil
subtitle: Where silver breaks and the void bleeds shadow

setting.name: The Silver Wastes
setting.description: The Silver Wastes are the outermost navigable region of the Astral Sea — a vast, luminous expanse of silver void stretching in every direction without horizon, floor, or ceiling. Here the Astral retains its ancient character: timeless, weightless, suffused with a sourceless silver glow that illuminates everything while casting no shadows. But the Wastes are not empty. Enormous chunks of solid matter drift through the void like islands in a cosmic archipelago — fragments of destroyed demiplanes, crystallized memories the size of houses, abandoned structures from civilizations that no longer exist, and stranger things: geometric impossibilities that hurt the eye, frozen moments of time visible as three-dimensional tableaux, and the occasional bone of a dead god tumbling end over end in majestic silence. The debris field thickens as one approaches the Threshold Citadel, the ancient monastery of the Astral Wardens, where ten thousand years of accumulated flotsam from a hundred planes has collected in a slow gravitational eddy around the fortress. Now the Wastes are changing. Convergence stress has fractured the silver void in places, and through those fractures other realities bleed: patches of Shadowfell darkness that swallow the silver light, fingers of Feywild green that sprout impossible vegetation on dead stone, veins of elemental fire that flicker and die in the airless void. The fractures are growing. The debris field around the Citadel has become a navigational hazard as chunks of matter are pulled toward convergence breaches and flung away again by competing planar gravities. And in the deeper darkness between the drifting islands, things are moving — predators drawn by the scent of weakened boundaries, raiders drawn by the promise of plunder, and stranger entities that seem to be convergence itself given form and hunger.
setting.atmosphere: The dominant sensation is vertigo — not the physical kind, but something deeper, existential. The absence of ground, sky, and horizon strips away every spatial reference point the mortal mind relies on, creating a persistent feeling of falling that never resolves. The silver light is beautiful but alien: it has no warmth, no direction, no source, and it reveals everything with a clinical clarity that makes shadows feel like a luxury. Sound behaves strangely in the Astral — whispers carry for miles while shouts are swallowed within feet, and the silence between sounds has a texture, a weight, as if the void itself is listening. Near the Threshold Citadel, the atmosphere shifts. The convergence damage is visible as chromatic distortion: patches of silver void that have turned bruise-purple where the Shadowfell bleeds through, veins of sickly green where Feywild energy leaks, and at the epicenter of the worst breach, a wound of absolute darkness that drinks light and radiates cold. The air — or whatever passes for air in the Astral — tastes of ozone and funeral ash near the breach. Characters feel the wrongness in their bones: a subsonic vibration, a sensation of reality stretching thin, like standing on ice and hearing it crack beneath your feet. The Astral's timelessness, normally a curiosity, becomes oppressive near the convergence zones — you cannot age, cannot hunger, cannot tire, but your mind screams that something is wrong, that the fabric of existence is fraying, and the calm of the void is the calm of a held breath before a scream.

keyLocations.name: The Planar Breach
keyLocations.description: The party's entry point into the Astral Sea — a wound in the boundary between the Material Plane and the silver void, torn open by convergence stress and held ajar by the silver compass's resonance with the Confluence fragment embedded in the Threshold Citadel's foundations. The Breach manifests differently depending on where the party was when they crossed: a crack in the sky that widened until it swallowed the horizon, a mirror that showed silver instead of reflection, a door that opened onto nothing and everything. On the Astral side, the Breach appears as a shimmering vertical disc of polychromatic light, thirty feet in diameter, suspended in the silver void with debris orbiting it in a slow spiral. The disc pulses with the rhythm of a heartbeat — the Material Plane's heartbeat, felt rather than heard — and looking into it reveals a fish-eye view of the world the party just left, already impossibly distant, already fading. The area immediately around the Breach is chaotic: gravitational eddies from the Material Plane's physics bleed through, creating pockets of normal gravity that yank unsuspecting travelers out of their thought-based movement and send them tumbling. Debris caught in the gravitational flux orbits the Breach in unpredictable patterns, and at least one piece of that debris is alive — an astral predator that has learned to hunt near Breaches, where disoriented newcomers make easy prey.
features: Gravitational Eddies — pockets of Material Plane gravity extend 60 ft from the Breach in random directions; characters entering an eddy must succeed on a DC 13 Dexterity save or lose thought-based movement for 1 round, falling 30 ft in the eddy's gravity direction; DC 14 Arcana to detect eddies before entering them

Debris Ring — chunks of stone, wood, metal, and stranger materials orbit the Breach in a 100-ft radius ring; provides three-quarters cover but requires DC 12 Acrobatics to navigate without collision; a collision deals 2d6 bludgeoning damage and knocks the character out of the ring

The Breach Portal — the shimmering disc itself; DC 16 Arcana to determine it is unstable and will seal within 1d4 days; passing back through returns to the Material Plane but only while the Breach remains open; the compass needle swings wildly near the portal before settling on a direction deeper into the Wastes

Astral Acoustics — the Breach amplifies sound from the Material Plane; faint echoes of the world left behind (birdsong, wind, distant voices) can be heard within 30 ft of the portal, creating a disorienting overlay on the Astral silence; DC 12 Wisdom save or become distracted (disadvantage on Perception) for 1 minute
encounters: 1 Astral Predator — a tentacled, translucent horror the size of a horse that lurks in the debris ring and ambushes newcomers emerging from Breaches; use the stats for a Cloaker (CR 8, HP 78, AC 14) reskinned as an astral entity with the following changes: its Moan ability causes psychic damage instead of fear, and its False Appearance mimics a chunk of debris rather than a cloak; it attacks the most disoriented party member first

Gravitational surge — the Breach pulses and emits a wave of Material Plane gravity; all creatures within 60 ft must succeed on a DC 14 Strength save or be pulled 20 ft toward the portal; creatures that reach the portal are shunted back to the Material Plane unless they succeed on a DC 15 Charisma save to resist
secrets: The Breach was not random — Zerith-Ka deliberately weakened this section of the planar boundary to create an entry point for the Threadwalkers; a DC 17 Arcana check near the portal detects traces of githzerai psionic manipulation woven into the Breach's edges, suggesting someone engineered this crossing

A small chunk of debris near the Breach contains a crystallized memory — a palm-sized piece of amber-colored crystal that, when touched, replays a brief vision: a githzerai monk (Zerith-Ka, though the party does not know this yet) standing at a crystalline window, watching cracks spread across the silver void, whispering 'It remembers. After all this time, it remembers what we were before we were separated. And it wants us back.' The crystal can be kept as a trinket

The Breach's instability means it will seal naturally within days, cutting off the party's easy return to the Material Plane — this information is available via the Arcana check above, but the full implication (they are stranded in the Astral until they find another way home) should dawn on the party gradually

keyLocations.name: The Silver Wastes Approach
keyLocations.description: The drifting debris field between the Planar Breach and the Threshold Citadel — a journey of several subjective hours through the Astral void, navigating between floating islands of dead stone, crystallized planar energy, and the wreckage of things that should not exist. The approach is both a navigational challenge and an introduction to astral movement: characters must learn to move by thought rather than muscle, using their Intelligence to propel themselves through the void and their Wisdom to maintain spatial orientation without a horizon. The debris field thickens as the party nears the Citadel, and the first signs of convergence damage become visible — cracks in the silver void that leak color and wrongness, drifting chunks of matter that are simultaneously stone and shadow, and the distant silhouette of the Citadel itself, its crystalline spires visible from miles away but clearly damaged, with dark fractures running through its luminous walls like veins of disease. The approach is not uncontested. Githyanki raider scouts patrol the Wastes in small skiffs — elegant, bone-white vessels powered by psionic energy — hunting for salvage and stragglers. And deeper in the debris field, convergence wraiths drift between the floating islands: entities born from the collision of the Astral and Shadowfell, neither fully alive nor fully dead, drawn to the warmth of mortal thought like moths to flame.
features: Thought-Based Movement — characters move through the Astral by willing themselves forward; speed equals Intelligence score x 3 feet per round in combat; during exploration, this translates to roughly 10 miles per subjective hour; characters with Intelligence below 10 move sluggishly and may need to be towed by allies (DC 12 Athletics to tow one creature at half speed)

Debris Navigation — the field contains hundreds of drifting objects ranging from pebble-sized to house-sized; DC 13 Intelligence (Arcana) check to plot a clear path; failure means a detour through a denser section (add 1 hour to travel and trigger one additional random encounter); natural 1 on the navigation check means a collision with a large chunk (3d6 bludgeoning damage, DC 14 Dex save for half)

Convergence Fractures — visible as chromatic distortions in the silver void; DC 14 Perception to spot at a distance; entering a fracture requires a DC 13 Wisdom save or the character suffers planar dissonance (confused for 1 round as contradictory physics assault the senses); Threadwalkers make this save with advantage; fractures radiate cold and wrongness in a 30-ft radius

Salvageable Debris — scattered among the floating junk are occasionally valuable objects; DC 15 Investigation to identify something worth taking during a short rest spent searching; possible finds include a cracked sending stone (1 use remaining), a vial of astral essence (functions as a Potion of Greater Healing), or a fragment of a planar map showing the location of nearby color pools

Spatial Disorientation — the Astral has no up or down; characters must make a DC 12 Wisdom save every subjective hour of travel or become spatially confused, perceiving allies as being in wrong positions (disadvantage on attacks and ability checks requiring spatial awareness for 10 minutes); can be ended early by touching a solid object and reorienting
encounters: Githyanki Scout Patrol — 2 githyanki warriors (CR 3, HP 49 each, AC 17 half plate) in a bone-white skiff; they hail the party in Common and demand identification; DC 15 Deception to bluff past them, DC 17 Persuasion to convince them the party is not worth their time; if combat begins, the warriors fight aggressively for 3 rounds then attempt to flee in the skiff to report to Captain Kra'zith; if both are killed, the skiff can be claimed (seats 6, moves at 60 ft/round via psionic propulsion, requires DC 14 Arcana to operate)

Convergence Wraith Pack — 3 convergence wraiths (use Wraith stats, CR 5, HP 67 each, AC 13, but replace Necrotic damage with Cold damage and add the following: their Life Drain creates a 5-ft radius zone of Shadowfell overlay that lasts 1 round, imposing disadvantage on Perception checks within it) drifting through the debris field; they are drawn to the party's life force and attack silently from concealment within convergence fractures; DC 16 Perception to spot them before they attack

Astral Current — a sudden surge of psychic wind sweeps through the Wastes; all creatures must succeed on a DC 14 Intelligence save or be carried 100 ft in a random direction; creatures carried into debris take 2d6 bludgeoning damage; creatures carried into a convergence fracture must immediately make the planar dissonance save
secrets: One of the drifting debris chunks is not debris at all — it is a small, abandoned githzerai meditation pod, spherical, about 10 ft in diameter, made of psychically-hardened crystal; inside is a dead githzerai warden who fell defending the Citadel weeks ago; their body carries a Warden's Sigil (a silver brooch that grants advantage on saves against planar dissonance) and a journal written in Gith that describes the Citadel's deterioration and Zerith-Ka's growing desperation; DC 15 Investigation to notice the pod among the debris, DC 13 Medicine to determine the warden died from convergence exposure rather than combat

The githyanki scouts are not operating independently — they are part of Captain Kra'zith's raiding flotilla, which has established a hidden camp in a large debris cluster approximately two hours from the Citadel; if a captured scout is interrogated (DC 15 Intimidation or DC 13 with telepathic communication), they reveal Kra'zith plans to assault the Citadel within days, exploiting the convergence damage to bypass the Wardens' defenses

A particularly large convergence fracture in the debris field contains a glimpse of the Shadowfell bleeding through — through it, characters can see a landscape of grey ash and dead trees under a sunless sky, and standing in that landscape, staring back through the fracture with hollow eyes, is a figure in tattered robes that mouths a single word: 'Coming'; this is a Shadowfell entity that will later emerge through the Convergence Wound in the Citadel

keyLocations.name: The Threshold Citadel
keyLocations.description: The monastery-fortress of the Astral Wardens — a structure of breathtaking beauty and terrible damage that serves as the party's base of operations for this scenario and the wider campaign. The Citadel was built ten thousand years ago by the first Astral Wardens: githzerai monks who renounced the eternal war between their kind and the githyanki to dedicate themselves to guarding the boundaries between planes. The structure is a masterwork of githzerai psychic architecture — walls of thought-hardened crystal that shimmer with captured starlight, towers that grow rather than were built, bridges of solidified will spanning chasms of open void within the fortress itself, and at its heart, the Observatory, where the boundaries between all planes can be observed and monitored. The Citadel was designed to be impregnable: a fortress of mind as much as matter, its defenses woven from the concentrated willpower of generations of psychic monks. But the Convergence has done what no army could. Stress fractures run through the crystalline walls like disease through bone. Entire wings have collapsed into the void or been swallowed by convergence zones — the eastern wing is now a hybrid space where Astral silver and Shadowfell darkness coexist in sickening overlay, and the things that emerge from that darkness are not entirely of either plane. The Citadel's psychic defenses are failing as the monks who maintain them are pulled away to fight convergence effects, seal breaches, and tend to wardens injured by planar exposure. Where once hundreds of wardens walked these halls, barely three dozen remain, and they are exhausted, afraid, and losing ground. The Citadel is not falling. It is being eaten, one room at a time, by the collision of realities.
features: Crystalline Architecture — the walls are translucent thought-crystal that responds to strong emotion; DC 13 Arcana to make a wall glow brighter (providing bright light in a 30-ft radius) or dimmer; the crystal also resonates with psychic energy, granting advantage on Intelligence checks made while touching the walls; damaged sections of crystal have turned opaque and dark, like cataracts in an eye

Psychic Defenses — the Citadel's remaining defensive wards create a sanctuary effect within undamaged sections: creatures within cannot be targeted by divination magic, and teleportation into the warded areas requires a DC 18 Arcana check; the wards are failing in damaged sections, creating gaps that the githyanki are exploiting

Void Chasms — the Citadel's internal architecture includes open chasms of Astral void crossed by bridges of solidified will; the bridges are stable but narrow (5 ft wide, no railings); falling off a bridge means falling into the Astral void within the Citadel (thought-based movement can arrest the fall with a DC 14 Intelligence check, but failure means falling 60 ft before catching yourself — 6d6 falling damage does not apply in the Astral, but the disorientation imposes disadvantage on all checks for 1 minute)

Warden Quarters — spartan cells containing meditation mats, crystal focus objects, and personal effects; each quarter has a small altar to Zerthimon (the githzerai philosophical hero); searching a quarter (DC 12 Investigation) reveals journals, training manuals, and personal histories that flesh out the Wardens' story

The Convergence Wound (eastern wing) — visible from the central courtyard as a wall of churning darkness shot through with flickers of silver; the temperature drops 30 degrees within 50 ft of the wound; shadow creatures drift near its edges; a DC 15 Perception check from the courtyard reveals the wound is growing — it has consumed another 10 ft of hallway since the party arrived
encounters: Githyanki Infiltrators — 3 githyanki warriors (CR 3, HP 49 each, AC 17) who have slipped through a gap in the psychic defenses and are sabotaging the Citadel's crystal infrastructure; they are planting psionic charges on load-bearing walls to accelerate the collapse; the party discovers them in a damaged corridor; the warriors fight tactically, using the damaged terrain for cover and retreating through the defense gap if reduced to half strength

Shadow Mastiff Pack — 4 shadow mastiffs (CR 2, HP 33 each, AC 12) that have emerged from the Convergence Wound and are hunting through the darkened eastern corridors; they attack in coordinated packs, using their Shadow Blend ability to become nearly invisible in the wound's darkness; they target isolated characters and avoid groups of three or more

Warden Sparring — not a hostile encounter; the remaining wardens train constantly in the central courtyard; a warden named Veth-Sora invites a party member to spar, which serves as a tutorial for astral combat mechanics (thought-based movement in combat, how Intelligence affects speed, and the absence of gravity); winning the spar (DC 15 contested Athletics or Acrobatics check, three rounds) earns Veth-Sora's respect and a minor boon: she teaches the character a githzerai breathing technique that grants advantage on one Wisdom save per long rest
secrets: The Citadel was built on the site of a sealed Confluence fragment — one of the original pieces of the pre-creation intelligence scattered across the Astral Sea; the Wardens did not build here by accident; their ten-thousand-year vigil was specifically to guard this fragment; the Convergence is not random damage to the Citadel — the fragment is waking up, and its awakening is what tore the breach in the eastern wing

Zerith-Ka is dying — not from age (githzerai are long-lived and the Astral halts aging entirely) but from psychic exhaustion; she has been personally holding the Citadel's failing defenses together through sheer force of will, pouring her own life energy into the wards; DC 17 Insight during conversation with her reveals the toll this is taking — her hands tremble, her silver eyes flicker, and she occasionally loses focus mid-sentence; she will not admit this weakness unless directly confronted with evidence

A hidden chamber beneath the Observatory (accessible via a concealed passage, DC 18 Investigation to find or revealed by Zerith-Ka if she trusts the party completely) contains the Wardens' greatest secret: a map of all known Confluence fragment locations, inscribed on a crystal sphere that shows the Astral Sea in miniature; the map shows five fragments, three of which are active and causing convergence zones; this is the campaign's roadmap

One of the remaining wardens, a githzerai named Kael-Thun, has been secretly communicating with Captain Kra'zith — not out of treachery but out of desperation; Kael-Thun believes the Wardens cannot hold the Citadel and has been negotiating safe passage for the surviving monks in exchange for allowing the githyanki to loot the Citadel's archives; DC 16 Insight during interactions with Kael-Thun reveals his nervous, guilt-ridden behavior; confronting him can either expose a traitor or reveal a sympathetic figure making impossible choices

keyLocations.name: The Convergence Wound
keyLocations.description: The eastern wing of the Threshold Citadel has been consumed by a convergence breach — a place where the boundary between the Astral Sea and the Shadowfell has collapsed entirely, creating a hybrid zone of silver light and absolute darkness that obeys the physics of both planes simultaneously. The Wound is not a portal or a doorway; it is a merger, a place where two realities occupy the same space and fight for dominance. Walking into the Wound means existing in both planes at once: you cast shadows in the silver light and glow with silver luminance in the darkness, and both versions of you are real, and both can be hurt. The Wound is approximately two hundred feet deep into the eastern wing and growing, consuming roughly ten feet of Citadel architecture per day. At its heart — the epicenter where the Confluence fragment's awakening tore reality apart — the merger is total: the walls are simultaneously crystalline thought-stone and Shadowfell basalt, the air is simultaneously silver radiance and funereal grey, and the creatures that inhabit this space are fusions of astral and shadow, neither fully one thing nor the other. Sealing the Wound is the party's primary objective in this scenario. Zerith-Ka believes that if the fragment at the breach's epicenter can be stabilized — not removed, not destroyed, but calmed — the Wound will stop growing and the Citadel's defenses can be restored. But reaching the epicenter means fighting through the Wound's hybrid horrors, navigating physics that change from room to room, and confronting the Shadowfell entity that has claimed the breach as its gateway into the Astral.
features: Planar Overlay — the Wound exists in both the Astral Sea and the Shadowfell simultaneously; characters inside perceive both realities overlaid on each other; the Shadowfell overlay imposes disadvantage on Charisma checks and saves (the plane's despair effect) unless the character succeeds on a DC 14 Wisdom save upon entry; this save must be repeated every 30 minutes spent in the Wound

Flickering Physics — the laws of physics alternate between Astral and Shadowfell rules in unpredictable waves; at the start of each round of combat in the Wound, roll 1d6: on 1-3, Astral physics dominate (thought-based movement, no gravity); on 4-6, Shadowfell physics dominate (normal gravity, normal movement, dim light only); this can change mid-combat, sending characters who were floating crashing to the ground (DC 13 Dexterity save or take 1d6 bludgeoning damage and fall prone)

Shadow Corruption — the Shadowfell's energy corrupts the Citadel's crystal architecture; corrupted crystal is dark, opaque, and brittle (AC 10, HP 5 per 5-ft section); it also radiates a 10-ft aura of dim light that cannot be brightened by nonmagical means; within this aura, healing spells restore only half their normal amount

Breach Epicenter — at the deepest point of the Wound, the Confluence fragment is visible: a sphere of white-gold light the size of a human head, embedded in a mass of merged crystal-and-basalt, pulsing with rhythmic energy that syncs with the Wound's expansion; approaching within 10 ft requires a DC 15 Constitution save or the character takes 2d8 radiant damage from the fragment's raw planar energy; the fragment can be stabilized with a DC 18 Arcana check performed as a 1-minute ritual while maintaining concentration (as if concentrating on a spell)

Echo Corridors — some hallways in the Wound replay echoes of past events; shadowy figures of wardens who died when the breach opened walk through the corridors, oblivious to the present; DC 14 Perception to realize they are echoes and not threats; DC 16 History or Religion to interpret the echoes and learn what happened when the breach first opened (the fragment pulsed, the wall shattered, and something came through from the Shadowfell)
encounters: Convergence Wraith Swarm — 5 convergence wraiths (use Wraith stats, CR 5, HP 67 each, AC 13, with cold damage replacing necrotic; their Life Drain creates a 5-ft zone of Shadowfell overlay lasting 1 round) defending the approach to the epicenter; they emerge from the walls in waves of 2, then 3, ambushing from both sides of a narrow corridor; in the flickering physics environment, they have advantage on attacks during Shadowfell-dominant rounds

The Breach Guardian — a Shadow Demon (CR 4, HP 66, AC 13) that has established itself as the apex predator within the Wound; it uses Shadow Stealth to hide in areas of dim light (which is most of the Wound) and strikes with hit-and-run tactics; it fights near the epicenter and attempts to prevent the party from reaching the fragment; if reduced to half HP, it attempts to possess a party member (DC 15 Charisma save) rather than fight directly

The Shadowfell Revenant — a powerful undead entity (use Revenant stats, CR 5, HP 136, AC 13, with the addition of a Shadowfell Wail: recharge 5-6, 30-ft cone, DC 15 Constitution save or 4d8 necrotic damage and frightened for 1 minute) that emerged through the breach and now claims the epicenter chamber; this is the entity glimpsed through the convergence fracture in the Wastes; it does not guard the fragment intentionally — it is drawn to the fragment's warmth like a creature freezing to death drawn to fire; it can potentially be reasoned with (DC 18 Persuasion, with advantage if the party offers an alternative source of warmth or light) but fights ferociously if attacked or if anyone tries to touch the fragment
secrets: The Confluence fragment is not merely a piece of a shattered intelligence — it is aware, in a limited, dreamlike way; characters who touch it experience a flash of overwhelming memory: the sensation of being part of everything, of all planes occupying the same space in perfect harmony, followed by the agony of separation as the gods carved the multiverse apart; this vision is beautiful and terrible in equal measure, and characters who experience it must succeed on a DC 16 Wisdom save or gain a long-term effect: they dream of unity every night for 1d4 weeks, and during that time they have advantage on Arcana checks related to planar boundaries but disadvantage on saves against being charmed by Confluence-aligned entities

The Shadowfell Revenant was once a mortal wizard who studied the planes — their tattered robes bear the sigil of a forgotten Material Plane academy; a journal fragment in their possession (DC 14 Investigation to find on the body after defeat or DC 16 Sleight of Hand to pickpocket during negotiation) describes experiments with planar boundaries that went catastrophically wrong, trapping the wizard in the Shadowfell where they died and rose as undead; the journal contains a partial formula for stabilizing convergence breaches that grants advantage on the DC 18 Arcana check to stabilize the fragment

Sealing the Wound does not destroy the fragment — it merely calms it, like soothing a crying child back to sleep; Zerith-Ka knows this and deliberately did not tell the party; she needs the fragment to remain in the Citadel because it powers the Observatory's ability to detect other fragments; if the party discovers this (DC 17 Insight when Zerith-Ka seems unsurprised by the fragment's survival, or by finding the hidden map chamber), it raises the first question of trust in the campaign: is Zerith-Ka manipulating the party, or is she making impossible choices to save reality?

keyLocations.name: The Warden's Observatory
keyLocations.description: The highest point of the Threshold Citadel — a domed chamber of flawless crystal that provides a three-hundred-and-sixty-degree view of the Astral Sea and, through the Observatory's unique enchantments, a view of the planar boundaries themselves. The Observatory was the Wardens' greatest achievement: a psychic instrument of extraordinary precision that allows the observer to see the boundaries between planes as physical structures — shimmering membranes of light stretched between realities, now visibly cracking and fraying like old cloth. From the Observatory, the scope of the Convergence crisis becomes terrifyingly clear. The party can see convergence zones spreading across the Astral like infections in a wound, each one a collision of planes that warps reality in its radius. They can see the silver void fracturing into competing colors as more and more planar boundaries fail. And they can see, distantly but unmistakably, the Spire of Echoes — a needle of crystallized light at the heart of the chaos, growing brighter as more fragments awaken. This is where Zerith-Ka shows the party the truth of their situation, gives them the silver compass, and sets them on their path. It is also where the party first glimpses the scale of what they face and must decide whether they are willing to walk into the breaking of the world.
features: Crystal Dome — the dome is made of a single piece of thought-crystal, 60 ft in diameter, perfectly transparent; it is nearly indestructible (AC 20, HP 300) but convergence stress has created hairline fractures that will eventually compromise it; the dome amplifies psychic ability — any character with psionic abilities or who casts a divination spell within the dome does so as if they were 2 levels higher

Planar Boundary Visualization — the Observatory's primary function; by touching the dome and concentrating (DC 12 Arcana), a character can see the planar boundaries as shimmering curtains of light; damaged boundaries appear as torn or fraying fabric; convergence zones appear as tangled knots where multiple curtains have collapsed into each other; the visualization is overwhelming for first-time viewers (DC 13 Wisdom save or be stunned for 1 round by the sheer scale of the multiverse)

The Star Map — a three-dimensional holographic display in the center of the dome, maintained by residual psychic energy; it shows the Astral Sea in miniature, with convergence zones marked as red pulses and Confluence fragment locations marked as golden points; the map is not complete (only fragments the Wardens have detected are shown) but it provides the party's first strategic overview of the campaign

Zerith-Ka's Meditation Platform — a raised crystal disc at the dome's apex where the ancient githzerai spends most of her time, maintaining the Citadel's defenses through meditation; the platform radiates calm (creatures within 10 ft have advantage on Wisdom saves against fear and despair effects); personal effects on the platform include a worn prayer book in Gith and a crystal sphere containing a preserved flower from the Material Plane — millennia old, still blooming

Communication Crystals — an array of smaller crystals around the dome's base that once allowed the Wardens to communicate with allied orders across the planes; most are dark (their counterparts destroyed or their planes disrupted by convergence); three still function: one connecting to a monastery in Limbo (the githzerai homeplane), one to an unknown location that transmits only static and screaming, and one that hums with a warm golden light but has never been activated in living memory
encounters: No direct combat encounters in the Observatory — this is a narrative and information scene; however, if the party visits the Observatory after sealing the Convergence Wound, the reduction in interference allows the Star Map to update, revealing a new fragment location and triggering the hook for the next scenario

Psychic vision — when the party first views the planar boundaries through the dome, each character experiences a brief, personalized vision related to their backstory or deepest fear; these visions are caused by the Observatory's psychic amplification interacting with the characters' subconscious; they deal no damage but should be unsettling and foreshadow future challenges; the DM should tailor these to each character
secrets: The golden communication crystal that has never been activated connects to the Spire of Echoes itself — the Confluence's reassembly point; it was placed there by the first Astral Wardens, who discovered the Spire's location ten thousand years ago and have been monitoring it ever since; activating the crystal (DC 20 Arcana) allows brief, cryptic communication with the nascent Confluence intelligence — which speaks not in words but in feelings of unity, loss, and longing

The Star Map contains a hidden layer of information accessible only to Threadwalkers — when a Threadwalker touches the map and concentrates (DC 15 Arcana), the display shifts to show not just fragment locations but thread-lines: luminous paths through the Astral that connect convergence zones in a web-like pattern; these threads are the remnants of the Confluence's original structure, and following them is faster and safer than navigating the open Wastes; this discovery grants the party advantage on all navigation checks for the remainder of the campaign

Zerith-Ka's prayer book, if read (DC 14 Intelligence check to read Gith, or comprehend languages), contains not prayers but letters — unsent letters to someone named 'Arath-Kel,' written over centuries, describing Zerith-Ka's loneliness, her doubts about the vigil, and her growing suspicion that the Confluence is not evil but merely lonely, like her; the letters reveal that Zerith-Ka's commitment to stopping the Convergence is complicated by a secret sympathy for the Confluence's desire for reunification; this is the campaign's deepest moral complexity, and it should not be fully understood until much later

synopsis: The Shattered Veil is the entry scenario for The Astral Convergence campaign — the story of the party's arrival in the Astral Sea and their first confrontation with the crisis that will define their journey across the planes. The party, marked as Threadwalkers by visions and the mysterious silver compass, crosses into the Astral through a breach in the planar boundary and finds themselves adrift in the Silver Wastes: the luminous, debris-strewn outer reaches of the Astral Sea where the Threshold Citadel — ancient monastery of the Astral Wardens — has stood guard over the planar boundaries for ten millennia. But the Citadel is dying. The Convergence — the awakening of Confluence fragments scattered across the Astral Sea, remnants of a pre-creation intelligence that seeks to reunify all planes of existence — has torn a wound in the Citadel's eastern wing where the Shadowfell bleeds through in a churning zone of merged realities. Githyanki raiders under the opportunistic Captain Kra'zith circle like vultures, probing the Citadel's failing defenses. And the Wardens, once hundreds strong, are reduced to a desperate few holding the walls through sheer force of psychic will. The party must navigate the debris-choked approach to the Citadel, earn the trust of the surviving Wardens and their ancient leader Zerith-Ka, fight through the Convergence Wound to stabilize the fragment tearing the Citadel apart, and glimpse the true scope of the crisis from the Warden's Observatory — where the shattered boundaries of the multiverse are visible as fraying curtains of light, and the Spire of Echoes gleams at the heart of the chaos like a needle through the fabric of reality. The scenario introduces the campaign's core mechanics (astral movement, convergence zones, Threadwalker abilities), its central NPCs (Zerith-Ka, Veth-Sora, and the githyanki threat), and its defining moral question: is the separation of the planes worth preserving, or is the Confluence's desire for unity something more than mere destruction?
hook: It begins with the dreams. Every night for a week, the same vision: a vast silver ocean without horizon or shore, and you are floating in it, weightless and breathless, and something enormous is out there in the silver — patient, aware, and reaching for you with a gravity that has nothing to do with mass. On the seventh night, the dream shatters. Cracks of impossible color rip across the silver void — jade, crimson, void-black — and through each crack another world bleeds into view: crystal forests, shadow cities, seas of liquid fire. The worlds are colliding, grinding together, and you feel it in your bones like the sound a glacier makes when it calves. You wake with a scream still in your throat, and the scream does not stop, because the ceiling of your room has turned to glass and through it you can see the Astral Sea — real, vast, and close enough to touch. A figure floats in the silver void above your bed: a githzerai monk, ancient beyond reckoning, her eyes burning with silver light. She extends a hand. 'The planes are falling into each other,' she says. 'You can feel it. Come.' Then the ceiling seals and she is gone. But on your nightstand, where nothing was before, lies a silver compass. Its needle spins, searching, yearning toward something beyond the sky. You know — with a certainty that sits in your chest like a second heartbeat — that you are meant to follow it.

acts.title: Act 1: Into the Silver
acts.description: The first act covers the party's transition from the Material Plane into the Astral Sea and their initial journey through the Silver Wastes to the Threshold Citadel. This is a disorienting, wonder-struck act that emphasizes the alien beauty of the Astral and the vertigo of existing in a reality without ground, gravity, or time. The party must learn to move by thought, navigate a debris field, survive their first encounters with astral threats, and process the overwhelming strangeness of their new environment. The act builds from the personal (crossing the Breach, losing contact with the Material Plane) through the dangerous (debris field navigation, githyanki scouts, convergence wraiths) to the awe-inspiring (first sight of the Threshold Citadel, damaged but magnificent). By the end of Act 1, the party should understand astral movement, have encountered both convergence effects and githyanki hostility, and be standing at the gates of the Citadel — marveling at its beauty and horrified by its wounds.
objectives: Cross the Planar Breach into the Astral Sea
Learn astral movement mechanics (thought-based propulsion, Intelligence-based speed)
Navigate the Silver Wastes debris field using the silver compass
Survive or avoid encounters with astral predators, githyanki scouts, and convergence wraiths
Reach the Threshold Citadel and make contact with the Astral Wardens

scenes.name: The Crossing
scenes.description: The party follows the silver compass's pull to the Planar Breach — the point where convergence stress has torn a hole between the Material Plane and the Astral Sea. The crossing itself is the party's first experience of planar transition: a moment of disorientation as gravity releases its hold, as air becomes silver light, as the world they knew recedes behind them like a ship leaving harbor. The scene should be equal parts wonder and terror, as the party grapples with the immediate reality of being adrift in an infinite void with no way back. The Breach is unstable, surrounded by gravitational eddies and orbiting debris, and an astral predator lurks in the debris ring, hunting newcomers who emerge dazed and disoriented from the crossing.
scenes.readAloud: The compass has led you here — to a place where the sky is wrong. You stand on solid ground, but above you the blue of the sky has thinned to translucence, and through it you can see something vast and silver shifting like an ocean viewed from below the surface. The compass needle no longer spins. It points straight up, trembling with urgency, and the warmth it radiates has become a pulse — a heartbeat that matches your own. As you watch, the sky cracks. Not like glass — like skin. A wound opens in the blue, edges curling back to reveal the silver void beyond, and the void is not empty. It breathes. It moves. It is alive with drifting shapes — chunks of stone, fragments of crystal, things that might be buildings or bones or frozen moments of forgotten time — all tumbling in slow, majestic silence through an infinite luminous nothing. The wound widens. Wind rushes upward, carrying dust and leaves and the smell of your world into the silver, and for a moment you are standing on the edge of everything, looking out at the space between all things. The compass lifts from your hand. It floats upward, spinning slowly, and the needle locks onto something deep in the silver void — something distant, something that calls. Then the ground beneath your feet turns to light, and you are falling upward. The world drops away below you like a stone into water, and the silver void opens its arms, and you are in the Astral Sea. There is no ground. There is no sky. There is no up or down or weight or wind. There is only silver, stretching in every direction forever, and you are floating in it like a mote of dust in a cathedral. Your body feels weightless — not the lurching weightlessness of falling but something gentler, as if gravity simply forgot about you. Breathing is strange: the air — if it is air — tastes of nothing and everything, like water from a spring that runs through every kind of stone. Around you, the debris field orbits the Breach in a slow spiral: chunks of rock, twisted metal, crystalline formations that catch the silver light and scatter it into rainbows. And somewhere in that debris, something moves — something that is not drifting but hunting, with the patient, purposeful motion of a predator in its element.

skillChecks.success: The character recognizes the Breach as a planar boundary rupture and understands that it is unstable — it will seal within 1d4 days, cutting off their easy return to the Material Plane. This knowledge allows the party to make an informed decision about whether to attempt to stabilize the Breach (DC 18 Arcana, 1 hour ritual) or accept that their return route will close.
skillChecks.failure: The Breach appears to be a stable portal. The character has no reason to believe it will close.

skillChecks.success: The character intuitively grasps thought-based movement — they can propel themselves through the void by concentrating on a direction. They move at their full astral speed (Intelligence score × 3 ft per round) immediately and can help guide allies who are struggling.
skillChecks.failure: The character flails in the void, unable to translate intention into movement. They drift 10 ft in a random direction each round until they succeed on this check or an ally physically guides them (DC 12 Athletics to tow).

skillChecks.success: The character maintains spatial orientation despite the absence of ground and horizon. They can reliably distinguish directions and judge distances, avoiding the worst of the Astral's disorienting effects.
skillChecks.failure: The character is spatially disoriented — up and down become meaningless, and estimating distance is impossible. Disadvantage on attack rolls and Perception checks for 10 minutes or until they touch a solid object and reorient.

skillChecks.success: The character spots the astral predator lurking in the debris ring before it can ambush the party — a translucent, tentacled horror pressed flat against a chunk of floating stone, nearly invisible against the silver void. The party is not surprised and can choose to engage, avoid, or prepare.
skillChecks.failure: The debris field appears empty except for inanimate flotsam. The predator attacks with surprise.

skillChecks.success: The character identifies the compass's pull as a navigational bearing and can determine the approximate direction and distance to whatever it points toward — roughly four hours of astral travel, bearing through the thickest part of the debris field.
skillChecks.failure: The compass points somewhere into the silver void. Without landmarks, the character cannot estimate distance or optimal route.

enemies: 1 Astral Predator (use Cloaker stats: CR 8, HP 78, AC 14; reskinned as a translucent tentacled horror; Moan ability deals psychic damage instead of causing fear; False Appearance mimics debris; has a fly speed of 40 ft in the Astral instead of its normal speed)
combatEncounters.tactics: The predator has hunted near Breaches for centuries and knows its territory perfectly. It uses False Appearance to hide among the debris, then ambushes the most isolated party member — preferably one who failed their movement or orientation checks and is drifting helplessly. It wraps its target in its body (Bite + attach) and attempts to drag them deeper into the debris field, using the floating chunks as obstacles to prevent the rest of the party from following easily. If the party is well-organized and fights back effectively, the predator releases its target and retreats into the debris, using hit-and-run tactics: attacking from concealment, dealing damage, then disappearing among the floating stones. It fights until reduced to 20 HP, then flees permanently. In the Astral environment, the predator has three-dimensional mobility and exploits it ruthlessly — it attacks from above, below, and behind, never approaching from an expected direction. Characters who have not yet mastered thought-based movement are at a severe disadvantage.
combatEncounters.terrain: Three-dimensional void combat around the Planar Breach. There is no ground — all movement is thought-based (Intelligence × 3 ft per round). The debris ring provides three-quarters cover but requires DC 12 Acrobatics to navigate without collision (2d6 bludgeoning on collision). Gravitational eddies within 60 ft of the Breach can disrupt thought-based movement (DC 13 Dex save or lose movement for 1 round). The Breach itself pulses periodically, emitting a gravitational wave that pulls creatures 20 ft toward the portal (DC 14 Strength save). The silver light provides bright illumination everywhere — there are no shadows for hiding except behind debris.

scenes.roleplayNotes: This scene is about awe and fear in equal measure. The party is leaving everything they know behind and entering a reality that operates on fundamentally different rules. Play up the sensory strangeness: the weightlessness, the silence, the silver light with no source, the taste of air that is not quite air. The Breach closing behind them should feel like a door shutting — not dramatic, just final. The astral predator encounter serves a mechanical purpose (teaching combat in three-dimensional void space) but should also reinforce the danger: the Astral is beautiful, but it is not safe. Nothing here evolved alongside mortals, and the things that live in the silver void do not think the way terrestrial creatures do. The predator is not evil — it is an ambush hunter doing what ambush hunters do. The party is prey until they prove otherwise. After the encounter, the compass pull intensifies, and the party should feel drawn forward — toward something enormous and ancient and in desperate need of help.
loot: Astral Predator remains: 2d4 translucent tentacle segments that can be used as spell components (each functions as a material component worth up to 50 gp); the creature's central nerve cluster is a fist-sized crystal that glows faintly and can be sold to a collector of planar curiosities for 150 gp or used as an arcane focus attuned to divination magic

Debris field salvage (if searched, DC 14 Investigation, takes 30 minutes): a cracked sending stone with 1 use remaining, a waterlogged journal in an unknown language (DC 16 Intelligence to identify as Gith — contains navigational notes about the Silver Wastes), and a small silver medallion shaped like a compass rose worth 25 gp
Crystallized memory fragment (see Planar Breach secrets): a palm-sized amber crystal trinket with no mechanical benefit but significant narrative value

scenes.name: Adrift in the Wastes
scenes.description: The journey through the Silver Wastes between the Breach and the Threshold Citadel — several subjective hours of navigation through the debris field, during which the party encounters githyanki scouts, convergence wraiths, and the growing evidence of convergence damage. This scene serves as a travel montage punctuated by encounters, allowing the DM to control pacing: the journey can be compressed into two or three key moments or expanded into a fuller exploration depending on the group's preferences. The key narrative beats are: learning to navigate by compass, encountering the githyanki threat (establishing them as a recurring antagonist faction), witnessing convergence damage firsthand (the fractures in the void, the wrongness bleeding through), and the growing spectacle of the Citadel as it emerges from the silver distance — beautiful and broken.
scenes.readAloud: Hours pass — or what feels like hours; time is a slippery thing in the Astral Sea, unmeasured by sun or stars or the body's rhythms. You do not grow hungry. You do not grow tired. Your muscles do not ache, your throat does not dry, and the sensation is profoundly unsettling — as if your body has been paused while your mind runs on, accruing experience without aging, thinking without the anchor of physical need. The compass leads you deeper into the debris field, and as you travel, you begin to understand the Astral's strange geography. The floating chunks of matter are not random — they cluster around points of gravitational or psychic significance, forming loose archipelagos separated by stretches of open void. Some clusters are merely rock and rubble, the detritus of shattered demiplanes. Others are stranger: you pass a frozen waterfall hanging in the void, its cascade suspended mid-flow, each droplet a perfect crystal of ice that has been falling for centuries and will fall for centuries more. You pass a fragment of a stone bridge, ornately carved, leading from nothing to nothing, with a single skeletal hand clutching the railing. You pass something that might once have been a tree, its branches now crystallized into fractal patterns that catch the silver light and shatter it into spectra that should not exist. And then, far ahead, you see it. The Threshold Citadel emerges from the silver distance like a sunrise — slowly at first, a glimmer of structured light among the chaos of drifting debris, and then with gathering clarity until the full scope of it becomes visible and steals the breath you do not technically need. It is enormous. Spires of luminous crystal rise hundreds of feet from a central mass of thought-hardened stone, connected by bridges of solidified will that arc between towers like the web of a divine spider. The crystal catches the Astral's silver glow and refracts it into colors: pale blue, rose gold, the green of deep water. It is the most beautiful structure you have ever seen. And it is dying. Dark fractures run through the crystal like veins of corruption. An entire section of the eastern wall has collapsed into churning darkness — a wound of shadow and wrongness that bleeds Shadowfell grey into the silver void. Even from this distance, you can feel the wrongness: a cold that has nothing to do with temperature, a heaviness in the chest, a whisper at the edge of hearing that says nothing and means despair. The compass needle locks onto the Citadel and burns warm against your palm, and you know — with absolute certainty — that this is where you are meant to be. The question is whether you will arrive before the darkness finishes what it started.

skillChecks.success: The character plots an efficient course through the debris field, avoiding the densest clusters and the most dangerous convergence fractures. Travel time is reduced by one hour, and the party avoids one random encounter.
skillChecks.failure: The route takes the party through a dense debris cluster where navigation is treacherous and encounters are more likely. Add one hour to travel time and trigger one additional encounter.

skillChecks.success: The character spots the githyanki scout skiff at long range — a bone-white vessel moving with purpose through the debris, clearly on patrol. The party has time to hide (DC 13 group Stealth), prepare an ambush, or change course to avoid the patrol entirely.
skillChecks.failure: The githyanki scouts spot the party first and approach with weapons drawn, demanding identification. The element of surprise belongs to the enemy.

skillChecks.success: The party conceals themselves among the drifting debris as the githyanki patrol passes within 100 ft. The scouts do not detect the party and continue on their route, providing the party with a clear window to observe githyanki patrol patterns.
skillChecks.failure: A piece of debris shifts at the wrong moment, revealing the party's position. The githyanki scouts change course to investigate.

skillChecks.success: The character reads the githyanki scouts' body language and recognizes that they are not a standard military patrol — they are scouts for a larger force, nervous and alert, checking specific locations as if mapping the Citadel's weakened defenses. This intelligence suggests a coordinated assault is being planned.
skillChecks.failure: The scouts appear to be a routine patrol. No deeper significance is apparent.

skillChecks.success: While passing through the debris field, the character notices a githzerai meditation pod among the floating wreckage — a small crystal sphere containing the body of a fallen warden and valuable intelligence about the Citadel's situation.
skillChecks.failure: The debris field appears to contain nothing of value — just the accumulated junk of millennia.

enemies: 2 Githyanki Warriors (CR 3, HP 49 each, AC 17 half plate; armed with greatswords and longbows; each carries 2 javelins sized for throwing in void combat)
combatEncounters.tactics: The githyanki fight from their skiff, using it as a mobile platform. One warrior pilots (the skiff moves 60 ft/round) while the other fires the longbow, switching roles every other round. They use the debris field for cover, weaving between floating chunks of stone while firing. If boarded, they abandon the skiff and fight in melee, using their innate psionic abilities (Misty Step 1/day each) to reposition. They fight for 3 rounds, then attempt to flee to warn Captain Kra'zith. Preventing both from escaping requires either killing them or disabling the skiff (DC 16 Arcana to disrupt its psionic engine, or 30 HP of damage to the hull). If one escapes, the Citadel assault in Act 3 occurs with the githyanki forewarned of the party's presence and capabilities.
combatEncounters.terrain: Open Astral void with scattered debris providing three-quarters cover. The githyanki skiff is a 15-ft long bone-white vessel with low gunwales (half cover for occupants). Movement is thought-based for non-vehicle travel. The nearest convergence fracture is 200 ft away and radiates visible chromatic distortion — the githyanki avoid it, suggesting they know its dangers. A large debris cluster (a shattered building fragment, 40 ft across) provides full cover and a potential ambush position 80 ft from the patrol route.

enemies: 3 Convergence Wraiths (use Wraith stats: CR 5, HP 67 each, AC 13; cold damage replaces necrotic; Life Drain creates a 5-ft Shadowfell overlay zone lasting 1 round — disadvantage on Perception within the zone; resistant to all damage except radiant and force while within a convergence fracture)
combatEncounters.tactics: The wraiths emerge from a convergence fracture as the party passes within 60 ft — rising from the chromatic distortion like swimmers breaking the surface of dark water. They attack silently, targeting characters who failed their spatial orientation checks first (those with disadvantage on attacks). The wraiths fight in the fracture's radius whenever possible, exploiting their resistance to most damage types. They use Life Drain to create zones of Shadowfell overlay, chaining the zones together to build a corridor of darkness that they can move through with impunity. If the party retreats from the fracture's radius, the wraiths pursue for 2 rounds, then return to the fracture — they are territorial and will not stray far from their convergence zone. Radiant damage and force damage are fully effective regardless of the wraiths' position and should be telegraphed as the key to fighting these enemies.
combatEncounters.terrain: The convergence fracture is a 30-ft radius sphere of chromatic distortion where Astral silver bleeds into Shadowfell darkness. Within the fracture: dim light only, the Shadowfell's despair effect (DC 14 Wisdom save or disadvantage on Charisma checks and saves), and Astral physics are disrupted (thought-based movement speed is halved). Outside the fracture: normal Astral conditions. The boundary between fracture and normal space is visible but not a physical barrier — creatures can move freely across it.

scenes.roleplayNotes: This scene establishes the journey and builds dread. The beauty of the Astral should be constantly undercut by the signs of convergence damage — every gorgeous vista is marred by a fracture, every moment of wonder interrupted by a reminder that this reality is breaking apart. The githyanki scouts introduce the second major threat: while the Convergence is an existential crisis, the githyanki are an immediate military threat, opportunistic raiders who see the Citadel's weakness as an invitation. The party should understand that they face enemies on two fronts. The convergence wraith encounter teaches the key mechanical concept of convergence zones: areas where the rules change, where different planes' physics overlap, and where the enemies have home-field advantage. Learning to fight in and around convergence zones is essential for the rest of the campaign. The first full view of the Threshold Citadel should be a showstopper — a moment of genuine awe that is immediately complicated by horror at the damage. The DM should spend time on this description. It is the party's first glimpse of what they are fighting to save.
loot: Githyanki equipment (if scouts are defeated): 2 greatswords (worth 50 gp each, fine githyanki craft with silver inlay), 2 suits of half plate (worth 750 gp each but sized for Medium humanoids — usable by party members), 4 javelins, 2 longbows with 40 arrows total, and a leather pouch containing 35 gp and a small obsidian figurine of a red dragon worth 50 gp (a githyanki good-luck charm)

Githyanki skiff (if captured intact): a bone-white vessel that seats 6, moves at 60 ft/round via psionic propulsion (DC 14 Arcana to operate), and provides half cover to occupants; this is a significant tactical asset for the remainder of the scenario and the campaign

Warden's Sigil (from the dead warden in the meditation pod, if discovered): a silver brooch that grants advantage on saves against planar dissonance effects; also contains the warden's journal with intelligence about the Citadel's deterioration

Convergence wraith residue: when a convergence wraith is destroyed, it leaves behind a small crystal of frozen shadow worth 25 gp each; a character proficient in Arcana can attune to one crystal during a short rest, gaining resistance to cold damage for 24 hours (one use, then the crystal dissolves)

scenes.name: The Gates of the Citadel
scenes.description: The party arrives at the Threshold Citadel and must gain entry through its failing defenses. The Citadel's outer wards — psychic barriers that once made the fortress impregnable — are still partially active, creating invisible walls of telekinetic force that bar unauthorized entry. The wardens manning the gates are exhausted, suspicious, and operating under orders to admit no one without Zerith-Ka's personal authorization. The party must convince the gate wardens that they are Threadwalkers — the allies Zerith-Ka has been calling for — or find another way inside. This scene introduces Veth-Sora, the young githzerai warden who becomes the party's primary contact and guide within the Citadel.
scenes.readAloud: The Citadel looms above you — or beside you, or below you; direction is a suggestion in the Astral, and the fortress seems to occupy all of them simultaneously. Up close, the damage is worse than it appeared from a distance. The crystal walls, which from afar seemed merely fractured, are visibly decaying: sections have turned opaque and dark, like dead coral, and in places the thought-stone has crumbled entirely, leaving gaps through which the silver void is visible. The eastern wing is a nightmare. The Convergence Wound is a churning wall of darkness shot through with flickers of silver — like a thundercloud that has swallowed a section of the fortress and is slowly digesting it. Even from here, two hundred feet away, you can feel its pull: a cold that reaches past your skin and into your thoughts, a whisper that promises nothing and means everything terrible. But the gates still stand. Two massive doors of thought-hardened crystal, fifty feet tall and inscribed with geometric patterns that pulse with dim psychic energy, seal the Citadel's main entrance. Before the doors, floating in disciplined formation on a platform of solidified will, stand four githzerai wardens in threadbare robes. They are thin, haggard, and armed — crystalline staffs humming with psionic charge — and they watch your approach with the wary alertness of soldiers who have been on watch too long. As you draw within hailing distance, the eldest of them — a scarred githzerai with one milky-white eye — raises a hand. The air between you and the gates solidifies into a barrier you can feel pressing against your chest: telekinetic force, invisible and unyielding. 'Hold,' the scarred warden commands, her voice carrying across the void with psychic clarity that bypasses your ears and speaks directly to your mind. 'The Threshold Citadel is sealed by order of Zerith-Ka, First Among Wardens. None enter without her word. Identify yourselves, state your purpose, and explain how you came to be in the Astral Sea — or turn back into the silver and do not return.' Behind her, a younger warden — barely more than a teenager by githzerai standards, with earnest dark eyes and hands that grip her staff too tightly — stares at the party with undisguised hope. She has seen the silver compass. She knows what it means. But she says nothing, waiting for her elder's lead.

skillChecks.success: The character explains their visions, the compass, and their journey convincingly. The scarred warden's expression shifts from suspicion to guarded hope. She lowers the barrier and sends the young warden — Veth-Sora — to escort the party inside while she sends a psychic message to Zerith-Ka.
skillChecks.failure: The scarred warden is unconvinced. 'Many have claimed to be Threadwalkers. None have proven it. Show us.' She demands a demonstration — the party must prove their connection to the planar boundaries (see Arcana check below).

skillChecks.success: The character channels their Threadwalker resonance — the same connection that allowed them to cross the Breach — and the silver compass flares with light. The geometric patterns on the Citadel's gates pulse in response, recognizing the resonance. The scarred warden's milky eye widens. 'Threadwalkers,' she breathes. 'After all these years. Zerith-Ka was right.' The gates open.
skillChecks.failure: The character attempts to demonstrate their connection but the resonance is too faint or unfocused. The wardens remain skeptical. The party may need to try another approach.

skillChecks.success: The character notices the young warden — Veth-Sora — staring at the compass with recognition and barely contained excitement. She clearly wants to help but is deferring to her elder. A direct appeal to Veth-Sora (even a glance or a nod) prompts her to speak up: 'Elder Thaan, the compass — it is a Warden's Compass. Only Zerith-Ka herself could have given it. They are who they say they are.'
skillChecks.failure: The party does not notice Veth-Sora's reaction and misses the opportunity for an easy ally.

skillChecks.success: The character makes clear — with force of personality, not threats — that the Citadel is under siege, the wardens are outnumbered, and turning away willing allies is a luxury they cannot afford. The scarred warden flinches. She knows it is true. 'Fine,' she says. 'But you are Zerith-Ka's responsibility. And if you are not what you claim, the Astral will be your grave.'
skillChecks.failure: The warden's jaw sets. 'Desperation is precisely when discipline matters most. You will wait here until Zerith-Ka confirms your identity. Or you will leave.' This adds a 30-minute delay while psychic confirmation is obtained — during which a githyanki scouting flight passes dangerously close.

skillChecks.success: The character recognizes the Citadel's gate inscriptions as an ancient githzerai psionic cipher — and can read a fragment of it aloud. The wardens are stunned. 'You know the old script?' the scarred warden says, suspicion replaced by astonishment. 'No outsider has read the old script in three thousand years.' This grants immediate entry and considerable respect.
skillChecks.failure: The inscriptions are clearly significant but unreadable. No additional insight gained.

enemies: If the party is delayed at the gates for 30+ minutes: a githyanki scouting flight passes — 3 githyanki warriors (CR 3, HP 49 each, AC 17) on individual astral skiffs (small, 1-person platforms, 80 ft/round); they do not attack directly but attempt to observe the party and the Citadel's gate defenses; if engaged, they fight defensively while one breaks away to report; the gate wardens assist the party, contributing 2d8 psychic damage per round from the platform (total, representing the 4 wardens' combined efforts)
combatEncounters.tactics: The githyanki scouts prioritize intelligence gathering over combat. They circle at 120 ft range, using longbows to test the party's defenses while one scout counts the gate wardens and maps the psychic barrier's extent. If engaged in melee, they use Misty Step to disengage and return to range. Their primary goal is to escape with intelligence — if all three are prevented from escaping, Captain Kra'zith's assault in Act 3 is conducted with incomplete information (the githyanki do not know the party's capabilities), granting the party a significant advantage.
combatEncounters.terrain: Open void before the Citadel gates. The gates themselves provide full cover. The warden platform provides three-quarters cover and a 30-ft elevation advantage. The psychic barrier (if still active) blocks movement but not projectiles or spells. The eastern wing's Convergence Wound is visible 200 ft away and the githyanki give it a wide berth — they fear it, which can be exploited.

scenes.roleplayNotes: This scene introduces two key NPCs. Elder Thaan (the scarred gate warden) represents the Wardens' institutional caution — she has seen false hope before and will not risk the Citadel on unproven strangers. She is not hostile, just exhausted and protective. Veth-Sora represents the Wardens' future — young, idealistic, desperate for the hope that Threadwalkers represent. She has studied the old texts and knows the prophecies; she believes in the party before they have proven anything. The dynamic between Thaan's skepticism and Veth-Sora's hope should mirror the party's own uncertainty: are they really Threadwalkers, or just mortals who stumbled through a crack in the sky? Once inside the Citadel, Veth-Sora becomes the party's guide and primary point of contact. She is earnest, brave, slightly awkward (she has spent her whole life in a monastery and has never interacted with non-githzerai), and fiercely loyal to Zerith-Ka. She should become a friend. Play her as someone the party wants to protect — because the campaign will test that bond.
loot: Warden's hospitality: upon entry, the party is given quarters in the Citadel's undamaged western wing; each room contains a meditation mat that functions as a bed (rest in the Astral is meditation-based), a crystal water basin that fills from nothing (the water tastes of mountain springs), and a small chest containing a set of Warden's Robes (comfortable, self-cleaning, worth 10 gp but priceless as a social signal within the Citadel — wearing them grants advantage on Charisma checks with wardens)

Veth-Sora's gift: once she trusts the party, she gives each member a small crystal wafer — a Warden's Token that, when broken, sends a psychic distress signal to the nearest warden within 1 mile; one use each; these become important in the Convergence Wound

Access to the Citadel's modest armory: the wardens' weapons and supplies are limited, but the party can requisition basic equipment, ammunition, and one uncommon magic item from the following: a +1 quarterstaff of githzerai make, a Cloak of Protection, or an Amulet of Proof Against Detection and Location

acts.title: Act 2: The Crumbling Vigil
acts.description: The second act takes place within the Threshold Citadel itself. The party meets Zerith-Ka, learns the full scope of the Convergence crisis, contends with internal threats (githyanki infiltrators, a potential traitor among the wardens), and prepares for the assault on the Convergence Wound. This act is heavy on roleplay, exploration, and investigation, with combat encounters that emphasize the Citadel's deteriorating situation. The party explores the fortress, builds relationships with the wardens, uncovers Kael-Thun's secret negotiations with the githyanki, and receives their mission from Zerith-Ka in the Observatory. The act culminates with Captain Kra'zith's assault on the Citadel — a siege that forces the party to choose: defend the walls or use the chaos as cover to enter the Convergence Wound while the wardens hold the line.
objectives: Meet Zerith-Ka and learn the full truth of the Convergence crisis
Visit the Observatory and witness the scope of the planar collapse
Explore the Citadel and discover the githyanki infiltrators' sabotage
Uncover Kael-Thun's secret communications with Captain Kra'zith
Survive Captain Kra'zith's assault on the Citadel and choose how to respond

scenes.name: Audience with the Ancient
scenes.description: Veth-Sora leads the party through the Citadel's damaged corridors to Zerith-Ka's audience chamber — a room of crystalline simplicity where the ancient githzerai receives them. Zerith-Ka is the oldest living githzerai, a being who has guarded the planar boundaries for millennia, and her presence fills the room with a quiet intensity that borders on gravitational. She is calm, precise, and honest to the point of brutality: she tells the party exactly what they face, exactly how dire the situation is, and exactly what she needs from them. She does not sugarcoat, manipulate, or inspire — she informs. Whether that information inspires the party or terrifies them is, in her view, their concern. After the briefing, she takes them to the Observatory to show them the truth with their own eyes.
scenes.readAloud: Veth-Sora leads you through corridors of luminous crystal, past doorways that open onto empty rooms and hallways that end in darkness where the Convergence has eaten through the walls. The Citadel is vast — you pass chambers that could hold hundreds, meditation halls with ceilings lost in shadow, and libraries of crystal tablets that hum with stored knowledge. All of them are empty or nearly so. The few wardens you pass are thin, focused, and busy — moving with the efficiency of people who have too much to do and not enough hands to do it. They glance at you with expressions that mix hope and assessment in equal measure. Veth-Sora stops before a door that is different from the others — smaller, simpler, made of plain stone rather than crystal. 'Zerith-Ka prefers simplicity,' Veth-Sora murmurs, and there is such reverence in her voice that the words sound like a prayer. She knocks once. The door opens on its own. The chamber beyond is small — thirty feet across, with a low ceiling and bare stone walls. There is no furniture except a single meditation mat and a crystal sphere that hovers at chest height in the center of the room, slowly rotating, its surface etched with lines that might be a map of something incomprehensibly large. And sitting on the mat, cross-legged, with her palms resting on her knees and her eyes already open and fixed on you, is Zerith-Ka. She is old. Not old the way mortals grow old — with sagging flesh and dimming eyes — but old the way stone grows old: worn smooth, refined down to essentials, every unnecessary thing eroded away by time until only the fundamental shape remains. Her skin is the deep grey of thunderclouds, lined with a filigree of silver that might be veins or might be cracks or might be something else entirely. Her eyes are silver — not the dull silver of old coins but the blazing silver of the Astral Sea itself, as if the void has taken up residence behind her pupils. Her hands, resting on her knees, are steady. Her voice, when she speaks, is quiet and carries the weight of absolute certainty. 'You followed the compass,' she says. It is not a question. 'I sent it to you because you can feel the boundaries — the membranes between planes that most mortals cannot perceive. We call this sensitivity Threadwalking. It is rare. It is necessary. And you are late.' She gestures, and the crystal sphere between you expands, its map-lines brightening until the room fills with a three-dimensional display of the Astral Sea — silver void, drifting debris, and scattered across it like wounds in flesh, the convergence zones: churning knots of color where planes have collided and fused. There are dozens of them. 'The planes are collapsing into each other,' Zerith-Ka says. 'The boundaries that separate realities — Astral from Shadow, Fey from Flame, Material from all of them — are failing. Not slowly. Not gracefully. They are being torn apart by something that remembers what existed before the boundaries were drawn.' She looks at you with those silver eyes, and in them you see not desperation but a patience so deep it borders on exhaustion. 'I have guarded these boundaries for nine thousand years. I have watched them crack before and mended them. But this is different. This is not damage. This is remembering. The thing that is tearing the planes apart is not a force or a creature — it is a memory. The memory of unity. And memories, once awakened, do not go back to sleep easily.'

skillChecks.success: The character perceives layers beneath Zerith-Ka's calm exterior — she is not merely tired but profoundly afraid, though she hides it behind millennia of discipline. More importantly, there is a note of something unexpected in how she describes the Confluence: not hatred or revulsion but something closer to understanding. She has spent nine thousand years studying the thing she opposes, and she has come to comprehend its perspective — perhaps too well. This observation should be noted for later significance.
skillChecks.failure: Zerith-Ka appears exactly as she presents: calm, authoritative, utterly in control. No deeper layers are apparent.

skillChecks.success: The character studies the crystal sphere map and identifies the convergence zones as following a pattern — they are not random but distributed along geometric lines that, if connected, would form a three-dimensional shape: a polyhedron, like a cage or a frame. This is the original structure of the Confluence, reassembling itself piece by piece. Understanding the pattern grants advantage on navigation checks when traveling between convergence zones.
skillChecks.failure: The convergence zones appear randomly distributed. No pattern is discernible.

skillChecks.success: The character recalls fragmentary references to the Confluence from ancient texts — pre-creation myths that describe a 'living equation' or 'the mind before minds' that organized reality before the gods divided it. These references are consistent with Zerith-Ka's description but add a crucial detail she did not mention: some texts describe the Confluence not as a tyrant but as a caretaker, and the separation of the planes not as liberation but as murder. This raises the campaign's central moral question.
skillChecks.failure: The character has no relevant historical knowledge. The Confluence is entirely new information.

skillChecks.success: The character notices Zerith-Ka's hands — steady on her knees but with a faint tremor that she controls through visible effort. The tremor worsens when she speaks about the Citadel's defenses. She is channeling her own life force to maintain the wards. This is confirmed by a brief flicker of her silver eyes — a momentary dimming that she covers by blinking.
skillChecks.failure: Zerith-Ka appears physically healthy, if old. No signs of strain are visible.

scenes.roleplayNotes: This is the campaign's pivotal exposition scene, and it must be handled with care. Zerith-Ka is not a quest-giver dispensing objectives from behind a desk — she is a nine-thousand-year-old guardian at the end of her strength, asking strangers for help because she has no other option. She is honest, direct, and respectful of the party's autonomy: she tells them what she knows, what she needs, and what she fears, but she does not command or manipulate. She answers questions truthfully, with one exception: she does not reveal that the Confluence fragment beneath the Citadel is what she is protecting, or that it powers the Observatory. She presents the mission as 'stabilize the breach so the Citadel can stand' rather than 'protect the fragment so I can use it.' This is not malicious deception — she genuinely believes the party does not need this information yet, and revealing the fragment's purpose might cause them to destroy it rather than stabilize it. But it is a lie by omission, and it should be discoverable. After the briefing, Zerith-Ka takes the party to the Observatory. This transition should be played for maximum impact: the walk through the Citadel to the Observatory dome, the climb to the apex, and the moment the party sees the planar boundaries for the first time — shimmering curtains of light, beautiful and fragile, cracking and fraying across the breadth of the Astral Sea.
